cap: After a flood or an earthquake, every building asks the same question.
Is anyone in there, and where?
A camera cannot see through a wall. So people are sent in blind.
Wi-Fi goes straight through a wall.
A person on the other side bends it, and the bent wave comes back.
We had no recordings, so we made 900 people who never existed.
Step by step, the network learns what a living body does to Wi-Fi.
The key was to train it on messy signals, with the chip’s own faults.
Example one. A person moves behind a wall.
On people it never saw, it finds 86.9 % of those who move. All in simulation.
Example two. An empty room: it stays quiet, 88.9 % of the time.
Run the first one again. The same answer.
A fan moves the air. It is not fooled.
The hard one: someone standing still. Radar and heat back it up.
It rides on a rover we built, from parts a school team can buy.
On the left, our model. On the right, the photograph.
And here is the real one, driving.
If it loses contact, it stops by itself in 0.4 seconds.
A whole search, start to finish. First, a drone maps the ground.
The rover goes in first, while people stay outside.
It plans its own way, past mud and loose walls.
It stops, goes quiet, and listens through the walls for ten seconds.
A hot pipe. Recognised, and ruled out.
Then the network hears someone.
Wi-Fi and radar agree. Twelve percent becomes ninety-four.
A second person, lying still. Radar and heat find them.
It plans the safe way in, around every hazard.
A person approves it. The team walks it.
Everyone it found is reached.
One reading is never enough. Every sensor moves the odds, in the open.
200 simulated missions: all 600 people found or flagged, no decoy called a person.
The plan draws itself, and the next team gets it on paper.
A whole mission, run twice: the same log, word for word.
Over two thousand checks run on your own computer, in front of you.
Then we break it on purpose. Cut the radio: it stops.
Blind its Wi-Fi: it refuses the reading, and listens again.
Behind the story, a full instrument: 24 workspaces, every number, every control.

What comes next: a drone with four senses.
Heat finds a warm body.
Laser measures the rubble, point by point.
And our network listens through it, from above.
Scans that find the spaces where someone could survive.
Eight machines, one search.
A collapse you can test before anyone lifts a beam.
Satellites that see the ground move.
And a radar that never transmits.
